summary:
Article 347-1 of Cameroon's penal code criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and women alike and carries a maximum of five years' imprisonment. The penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts; an ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1, and the 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Sentences under the earlier provision ran from six months to five years.

Enforcement reaches gender presentation, not only alleged acts. On 8 February 2021 in Douala, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. They spent five months in prison, were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, and received five-year sentences, the maximum statutory term, before a judge released them until their appeals could be heard. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a following on Facebook and YouTube discussing trans life and has since left the country to claim asylum abroad.

Appearance-based prosecutions predate that case. In November 2011 two young men were convicted solely on the basis of their dress, their manner of speech and the ordering of a cream-based liquor, and sentenced to five years; an appeals court acquitted them on 9 January 2013, and their lawyer Alice Nkom stated that the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. On 24 November 2011 three young men received five-year sentences for oral sex in a parked car. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison.

Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime creates a separate offence. Article 83(1) punishes same-sex sexual propositions made through electronic communications with one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or either penalty alone, and Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where sexual intercourse follows.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that since 9 March of that year security forces had arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and that gendarmes beat two detainees. Ilaria Allegrozzi, a senior researcher at the organisation, stated that the criminalisation law lets civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

Coercive state contact with detainees is documented. In May 2005 eleven men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy were threatened with medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity; they were detained into February 2006, trials were scheduled for March 2006, and they were released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347.

Prison conditions bear directly on the exposure a sentence creates. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as 'hell', and Kondengui Central Prison appears in the record as a serving location for a conviction under the same provision. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. The US Department of State's 2010 human-rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gay and lesbian people by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort them, and a foreign broadcaster's report of 12 May 2021 stated that beatings of gay and transgender people in public were common.
tangentialFactors:
Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise same-sex conduct, according to a foreign broadcaster's report of 12 May 2021. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, representing Shakiro and Patricia, called the five-year sentence a political decision taken with no proof of any act.

In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, which boosted circulation and drew criticism from the state communication council for invading privacy. President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy while the state continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity.

On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter, Brenda Biya, came out as a lesbian on Instagram, an act that produced national backlash and was reported to have given hope to LGBTQ Cameroonians.

Official statements have contested the scale of prosecution. In July 2010, after the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary argued that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon'.
localsOnly:
Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, was forced to shut down after a police raid, removing a service base from the country's support infrastructure.

Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases, which narrows the defence available to residents as well as visitors facing charges.

The 2006 publication of names by tabloids exposed at least 50 prominent residents to public identification as homosexual, and the state communication council's criticism of that reporting addressed privacy rather than the underlying prosecutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
No visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers to Cameroon is described in the available material. The nearest material concerns outbound asylum and foreign border practice: a foreign government's grant of an asylum right to a gay Cameroonian man in July 2010, an airline's refusal in August 2011 to carry a gay Cameroonian man to Yaoundé, and a foreign border agency's May 2012 attempt to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde after finding 'no credible evidence' that he was gay. Whether Cameroon applies any entry rule to LGBTQ travellers remains unresolved and not sourced.

No Cameroonian border screening procedure, including any document-marker flagging or secondary screening triggered by gender presentation, is set out in the inventory.

No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or identity-document and marker procedures appears anywhere in the available material.

Healthcare, HIV and medication access for transgender visitors is not described. The only service-related findings are institutional: the closure of Alternatives-Cameroon after a police raid, the shortage of lawyers, and the 2005 threat of medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among detained men, which represents coercive contact with health services rather than care.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is documented; the only youth-adjacent material in the inventory is historical ethnography and does not bear on travel.

No trans-specific homicide or violence figure with a denominator is sourced for Cameroon, so no comparison against the country's general homicide rate can be stated.
